chapter: Donaldsonville, family and Richard M. Jones
title: Strings, banjos, reeds and the Foster family in Williams's band
summary: Violin, bass, the LeBlanc banjo family, clarinet and sax players, and the Foster family.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation

blocks.x: Well, who played the different strings? Did they have any violins with Clayman Williams?

Clayman was the violin player himself. Now, I don't know. I don't remember Jill. Jill, that's Clayman's brother. He was the one who played the string bass. His right name was Jewel Williams. We called him Jill. I guess that's the nickname. Jill always played the string bass. You know, the right string bass. But Clayman, the only violin man I ever heard in Clayman's band was him.
And later years he stopped, you know. Did they have any guitars or bands?

They had the band. They had the, Martin, oh, Alan LeBlanc. You got him? No. That's the banjo player. Alan LeBlanc. And when Alan LeBlanc retired, his son took over in the band. Martin L. LeBlanc. And what did he play? Banjo too. Mm-hmm. Everybody carried it on in the family. Then he had another son played in that band by the name of Alton LeBlanc. This banjo player. Yeah, the music family. And Alton LeBlanc played?
We played the. Tell us, I should have fun. Mm-hmm. Let's see, we got drummers, pianos, drums. How many clarinets did they have?

We had Marlon Gibson on clarinet. You ever heard of him? Yeah. That was Poesy Gibson's brother. Poesy Gibson was a trombone player in that band along with Freddie Landry. Yeah. Gee, that was the fifth band for that time. I told you that most people had around 12 or 13 pieces.
Now Marlon Gibson, where did he play? Clarinet and saxophone? Clarinet and saxophone. Which sax? Alto or tenor?

You see, he was in that band before he had the tenor. That was before Alton LeBlanc. Mm-hmm. I see. You see, after he died, then Alton LeBlanc come in. Have any alto players or baritone players? Yeah, they had, they had, on the alto they had, this man I called from out of the Poetry Innville. You say he taught, he taught Jim Robinson. Ernest Hines. Ernest Hines was on the alto side of the phone. Yeah. You see, George was too small then. They had George Williams, the son, they had him along with him on the C Melody. Mm-hmm. Clarinet, you know what a C Melody phone is. They had George on the C Melody.

Did you ever see Billy Kersams? That's before my time. Yeah. I heard of Billy Kersams and Black Patty, but I... Yeah, I heard about him from playing up there from somebody. Maybe Charlie Love or somebody told me about him. That's way before my time. It's so, it's so hard to keep all that straight, all those guys. Well, I guess that just about covers Clarinet Williams except...

Yeah, yeah, I don't remember George Foster from out there. I don't remember George Foster and his brother. Willie? Willie. I know, I met Willie at Papa John's shop. He was a bricklayer or a plasterer or something like that. But now right after that he came there and told us he was going to Baton Rouge. That's the last I heard of Willie Foster. But I don't know George, but I know they got a sister. But she died. She was living right at the next corner. Oh, yeah? She was a friend of my mother. She played a lot of guitar. Mm-hmm. But they're from McCall, Louisiana. Oh, yeah. And McCall is a mile from a... from a mile. I'm probably out there now. Oh, yeah? Sure.
She played guitar. Did she play in jazz bands or the sister? No. Sister.
She was in church. But they tell me that back in the old days they had a family band. That's how that band started. I heard of them. That's what I heard, yeah.
